base_prompt: Explain how a city's street names can function as an unofficial record of its changing priorities. Please answer in roughly 200 words.
text: A city’s street names can act as an unofficial record of its changing priorities because they preserve the people, events, values, and institutions that local leaders and communities have chosen to honor. Older names may reveal colonial origins, religious influence, military victories, industrial development, or prominent political figures. As society changes, renamed streets can show attempts to reject oppressive histories, recognize previously marginalized groups, or promote a new civic identity. A road once named for a colonial official might later honor an independence leader, while an avenue commemorating a monarch could be renamed after a civil rights activist. New streets also reflect current priorities: names connected to technology, environmental protection, cultural diversity, or local Indigenous languages may indicate what a city wants to celebrate in the present. The geography of naming matters as well. Streets concentrated around government buildings may emphasize national power, whereas names in newer neighborhoods might highlight community leaders, artists, or ecological themes. Disputes over renaming reveal that public space is not neutral; residents debate whose contributions deserve visibility and which histories should remain publicly remembered. Although street names rarely provide a complete or objective account, their layers of continuity and revision allow observers to trace shifts in power, identity, and collective memory. In this way, an ordinary address can quietly document a city’s evolving understanding of itself.
